item.title: Belvedere issues Mallard Pointe bulkhead permit, clearing way for demolition
item.description: Belvedere issued the Mallard Pointe bulkhead permit Oct. 1, the last city approval before demolition, as the lagoon association blocks a silt curtain on one stretch.
item.content:encoded:
Belvedere on Oct. 1 issued the last city permit the Mallard Pointe developer needed before tearing down the complex’s 22 apartments, though the lagoon association’s refusal to let a silt curtain into its water has blocked work on one stretch of shoreline.

The bulkhead permit covers replacing the bulkhead along the Belvedere Lagoon edge of the 1-22 Mallard Road site with vinyl sheet piling capped with wood. The demolition permit was issued July 15, but the city has said demolition could not begin until the bulkhead permit was also issued.

The permit names Midstate Construction of Petaluma as contractor, values the work at $500,001 and carries $14,531.38 in city fees. It must be finaled by April 1, 2028.

City staff, the city’s peer reviewers and Foth, the Petaluma firm Belvedere hired in September as project coordinator, will inspect the work, the city said.

Lagoon association denies silt curtain

The permit came the same day the city answered a Sept. 17 letter from the Belvedere Lagoon Property Owners Association, which owns the lagoon and had asked that seven recommendations be written into the permit as enforceable conditions.

The developer’s latest plans pulled the new bulkhead entirely onto Mallard Pointe’s own land. But the silt curtain required for one portion of that work — a floating barrier meant to keep churned-up mud from spreading — still has to sit in the association’s lagoon.

The association has denied permission to access or place materials on its property, the city said, and work on that portion of the bulkhead cannot begin until the developer either wins the association’s authorization or finds another way to control sediment that satisfies the California Department of Fish and Wildlife.

“This is an encroachment issue between two private property owners, and as such, the city cannot enforce this approval,” the city’s response states.

The city did not adopt the association’s request that demolition be tied, area by area, to finished sections of bulkhead, and its response does not address the association’s call to hold off demolition until April 15, 2027.

Work must finish by Oct. 15

Fish and Wildlife’s agreement for the project requires all of the covered work to be finished by Oct. 15, though the department can grant week-by-week extensions in dry weather.

item.title: Fire crews drill at Belvedere's Mallard Pointe complex through Oct. 12
item.description: Tiburon Fire and other agencies will train at the vacant Mallard Pointe apartments in Belvedere Oct. 2-12 before demolition. No live fire will be used.
item.content:encoded:
Firefighters from the Tiburon Fire Protection District and other local agencies will train at the vacant Mallard Pointe apartments in Belvedere Oct. 2-12, ahead of the complex’s demolition.

Crews will practice forcible entry, victim searches, hose lays, fire attack and vertical ventilation — cutting openings in a roof to release heat and smoke — at the 1-22 Mallard Road site, according to a notice the city received from Travis Terrell, the district’s A-shift training battalion chief.

No live fire will be used. Neighbors may see more fire engines and firefighters in the area, and the activity is not an emergency, the city said.

Belvedere issued the bulkhead permit Oct. 1, the last city approval the developer needed before tearing down the 22 apartments to make way for 40 homes.

item.title: Election 2026: Reed schools’ Measure O seeks $115 million bond for campus repairs
item.description: Voters will decide Nov. 3 on Measure O, a $115 million bond to repair and upgrade the Reed Union School District’s three schools.
item.content:encoded:
Voters will decide Nov. 3 on Measure O, a $115 million bond to repair and upgrade the Reed Union School District’s three schools.

Measure O needs 55% approval to pass. The tax would be levied on properties in the district, which includes Tiburon, Belvedere and east Corte Madera, starting in fiscal year 2027-2028, when the district expects the rate to peak at $30 per $100,000 of assessed value. That works out to $300 a year for every $1 million of assessed value.

Two parcel taxes on the same ballot would also reach district property owners: Measure P, a 15-year countywide childcare tax of 5 cents per square foot of building, and Measure CC, a 30-year Marin Healthcare District tax of 14 cents a square foot to expand MarinHealth Medical Center’s emergency room and intensive care. Together they would cost the owner of a 2,000-square-foot house $380 a year.

Election 2026: Read complete coverage at thearknewspaper.com/election2026

The district estimates the rate would average $26.63 per $100,000 over the life of the bonds, with the tax collected for the last time in fiscal 2060-2061. The levy would raise about $6.2 million a year, according to the ballot question, and the district’s tax rate statement estimates that repaying the full $115 million would cost $213 million in principal and interest.

No bond money can be used for teacher or administrator salaries, and the measure requires a citizens’ oversight committee and annual independent audits. The measure’s text also says the money must be spent on the district’s schools and cannot be taken by the state or county.

Reed Union School District board President Shelby Pasarell Tsai said the bond measure was important because systems at the district’s three campuses — Reed and Bel Aire elementary schools and Del Mar Middle School — need serious work, from leaking and failing roofs to degraded clay pipes and irrigation.

“Anyone who owns a home knows after 20 years, buildings need some pretty serious maintenance,” Pasarell Tsai said.

Pasarell Tsai is the lead author of the ballot argument in favor of Measure O, which she signed with Jessica Etchevers, president of the district’s PTA; former school board member A.J. Brady; Belvedere Councilmember Jane Cooper; and Tiburon Councilmember Jack Ryan. Pasarell Tsai, Cooper and Ryan are all seeking reelection Nov. 3.

No argument against Measure O was filed with the Marin County Elections Department.

item.title: Tiburon resident, educator helps bring Native American culture to community
item.description: Tiburon’s Eddie Madril, an assistant professor at San Francisco State and founder of Sewam American Indian Dance, is co-organizing the town’s Native American celebration Oct. 11.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon resident Eddie Madril thought he was going to be an architect.

He studied calculus and physics and says he envisioned himself working on the 40th floor of a San Francisco or New York high-rise.

Madril ended up as an educator focusing on Native American culture, but he says his expertise didn’t necessarily begin with scholarly research and book reading.

“It came from just a life, over 45 years of experience being in the community, understanding and being … in the same rooms where things that were discussed on legalities, customs, traditions, ceremonies, art, dance, music — all of this stuff,” he says.

Madril is an assistant professor in San Francisco State University’s American Indian studies department and the founder of the Sewam American Indian Dance group, which has performed in the U.S. and abroad, including in 2025 at the 51st Festival of World Cultures in Gannat, France, an event that partners with UNESCO.

Madril is also a co-organizer of Tiburon’s second celebration of Native American culture and heritage, scheduled for 1-4 p.m. Oct. 11 — the day before Indigenous Peoples Day — at Zelinsky Park between Town Hall and the Belvedere-Tiburon Library.

item.media:description: Ellie Madril, Sara Moncada and Eddie Madril sit in Tiburon’s Zelinsky Park Sept. 27. Madril and Moncada co-direct Sewam American Indian Dance, which will perform with Ellie at the town’s Native American celebration in the park Oct. 11. (Leo Leung / For The Ark)

item.title: Election 2026: Community engagement, fiscal oversight define Strawberry Recreation District race
item.description: Doug Twillman, appointed to the Strawberry Recreation District board last year, faces challenger Aliza Hawkins Nov. 3 for the district’s open two-year seat.
item.content:encoded:
The two residents who sought a vacant Strawberry Recreation District board seat last year are running for the same seat Nov. 3, this time before voters.

The board picked Doug Twillman, a finance veteran and triathlete, on a 3-1 vote in September 2025. Aliza Hawkins, a marketing professional, mother of two and certified counselor, is challenging him in a rare contested election for a district that has historically struggled to find candidates.

Twillman and Hawkins are vying for the one open two-year seat. Incumbents Peter Teese, Sohrab Saghezchi and Sarah Waterfield, along with newcomer David Morgenthaler, will compete for three open four-year seats. Board members receive $100 per regular meeting, with a maximum of $500 per month.

Election 2026: The Strawberry Recreation District two-year candidates at a glance

Election 2026: Read complete coverage at thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Established in 1949, the Strawberry Recreation District is an independent special district serving about 6,000 residents in areas of unincorporated Mill Valley and unincorporated Tiburon east of Highway 101. In addition to the rec center and headquarters on East Strawberry Drive, it maintains four parks, a public dock, several walking trails and the Water Tank Hill open space.

According to the district, it receives 3.5 cents per dollar of basic property tax paid to Marin County, roughly 15% of its annual revenue. The rest, about $3 million, comes mostly from fees for classes, facility rentals and memberships.

The district hired playground company GameTime in July under a $2.4 million contract to build a playground on grass between the tennis courts and baseball fields at Strawberry Park. A revised quote and a separate bid for a restroom pushed the total past $3 million on Sept. 8, and the board told the company to come back under its $2.5 million ceiling. The district plans to break ground in 2027.

Aliza Hawkins: Challenger wants more residents involved

Hawkins, 39, said she would focus on drawing more residents in and on inclusive programming. She describes herself as social, outgoing and deeply connected to Strawberry.

She moved to Strawberry from Southern California with her husband, James, and their two children about 2½ years ago. The family bought a home near the recreation center last year.

item.title: Election 2026: The Strawberry Recreation District two-year candidates at a glance
item.description: The Strawberry Recreation District two-year candidates at a glance
item.content:encoded:
Aliza Hawkins, challenger

Years as resident: 2½.

Occupation: Former senior account specialist at Rakuten Advertising and certified counselor.

Education: Bachelor’s degree in business administration and a master’s degree in counseling, both from The Master’s University.

Civic background: Marriage and family counselor at Lighthouse Community Church in Torrance from 2019 to 2021.

Key issues: Community engagement and inclusive programming.

Quote: “We want our kids to grow up in a community that’s not just people who have kids and people who have young kids, but really a diverse representation of ages and different stages of life.”

Doug Twillman, incumbent

Years as resident: 27.

Occupation: Financial analyst and consultant in commercial real estate.

Education: Bachelor’s degree in mechanical engineering from the University of California at Davis and a master’s degree in business from the University of San Francisco.

Civic background: Appointed to the Strawberry Recreation District board in September 2025; member of San Francisco’s Olympic Club, where he chaired the investment committee from 2012 to 2014.

Key issues: Fiscal oversight and completing the new playground.

Quote: “The budget should be well understood so that we can hold the contractors accountable and the community can hold us accountable for a successful physical and fiscal outcome.”

item.title: Local stories take the screen as Belvedere Home Made Film Festival returns
item.description: About 30 short films screen at the third annual Belvedere Home Made Film Festival, which begins at 6 p.m. Oct. 9 at Belvedere Community Park.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon resident Mark Freiberg looked outside his bayside window one day in 2024 and noticed an unusual boat. There in Paradise Cay, among the other ships he watches daily, was a small towboat.

“I saw this little boat, and I’ve got to say, it’s an odd-looking boat,” Freiberg said. “I just got very curious about it.”

That curiosity grew when the boat began working near the Corinthian Yacht Club that year. Its extended stay gave Freiberg opportunities to speak with crew members and meet the boat’s owner. He also recorded some footage of the boat from the air with his drone camera.

This spring that footage became the raw material for “P Cay” — Freiberg’s short video submission to the third annual Belvedere Home Made Film Festival. The family-friendly festival will screen about 30 short films by community members, each three minutes or less, at 6 p.m. Oct. 9 at Belvedere Community Park.

The free event invites families to bring blankets and sit on the lawn to watch the show, which will also include live music by the Windsor Street Blues Band, popcorn, hot cocoa and homemade soup. The band plays at 6 p.m., and the films will start about 7. A drop-off point and limited seating will be available on Community Road for older adults and people with mobility concerns. Before the festival, Be Ready Belvedere, the city’s emergency-preparedness working group, will hold a shelter-in-place event from 5 to 6 p.m. at the park. Volunteers will hand out stay-box supplies to Belvedere residents registered with AlertMarin and help others sign up.

They are among about 30 films in the Belvedere Home Made Film Festival, which begins at 6 p.m. Oct. 9 at Belvedere Community Park. (Screengrabs from video)

item.title: Tiburon’s Cinelounge to host Bruce Dern for inaugural fundraising gala
item.description: Academy Award-nominated actor Bruce Dern will be the guest of honor Nov. 5 at the first fundraising gala for a new nonprofit supporting Tiburon movie theater Cinelounge.
item.content:encoded:
Academy Award-nominated actor Bruce Dern will be the guest of honor Nov. 5 at the first fundraising gala for a new nonprofit supporting downtown Tiburon movie theater Cinelounge.

The evening runs 5:30-9:30 p.m. at the theater and includes a reception ahead of a screening of “Dernsie: The Amazing Life of Bruce Dern,” a documentary about his life that debuted earlier this year at the Cannes Film Festival. The screening, limited to 60 people, will be followed by a conversation with Dern and “Dernsie” director Mike Mendez. Reception-only tickets are also available.

“When you have talent like this, … and they come to Tiburon, it’s a once-in-a-lifetime event,” says Christian Meoli, who owns the theater with his wife, Camilla Meoli. “And (Dern) has such an amazing track record of working in the business in films for, I mean, my God, almost, over seven decades that we also thought that he was a great fit for the demographic in Tiburon.”

item.title: Alameda County’s Heather Marques to lead Southern Marin Fire District
item.description: Alameda County Fire division chief Heather Marques will take command of the Southern Marin Fire Protection District, which serves Strawberry and northern Tiburon, on Oct. 13.
item.content:encoded:
Alameda County Fire Department division chief Heather Marques will lead the Southern Marin Fire Protection District, the fire agency for Strawberry and northern Tiburon.

Marques, 52, will take command Oct. 13, succeeding Christian Tubbs, who retired July 1 after more than 11 years as chief and 47 years in the fire service. Tom Welch, a former Mill Valley fire chief and onetime Southern Marin deputy chief, has led the district on an interim basis since June 29 and will return to retirement.

The district’s seven-member board unanimously approved her three-year contract Sept. 23. It pays an annual base salary of $285,000.

“Chief Marques brings a strong combination of operational experience, executive leadership, regional knowledge and a genuine commitment to the people and communities we serve,” Board President Cliff Waldeck said in the district’s announcement.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister

item.title: Election 2026: Two of five Tiburon Town Council candidates report donors; measures P, CC near $1.2 million
item.description: Faris Jafar and Chuck Hornbrook are the only two of Tiburon’s five Town Council candidates to report donations in campaign-finance disclosures due Sept. 24.
item.content:encoded:
Investment-fund founder Faris Jafar and Parks, Open Space & Trails Commissioner Chuck Hornbrook are the only two of Tiburon’s five Town Council candidates to report donations from supporters in preelection campaign-finance disclosures due Sept. 24.

Jafar leads in monetary contributions for the first reporting period with $4,198.44, including $1,523.44 of his own money, against $1,536.56 in spending.

Hornbrook is second in monetary contributions with $3,250, including $500 of his own. Counting a loan of $1,145.08 he made to his campaign and then forgave, his total contributions reach $4,395.08, against nearly $1,651 in spending.

Election 2026: Read complete coverage at thearknewspaper.com/election2026

The California Fair Political Practices Commission requires two preelection campaign-finance disclosures from candidates who raise or spend $2,000 or more. The first, due Sept. 24, covers July 1-Sept. 19. The second, due Oct. 22, covers Sept. 20-Oct. 17.

Incumbent Councilmember Alice Fredericks’ campaign reported the most in total contributions of the five candidates, all of it a $5,247 loan she made to her campaign.

Planning Commissioner Kathleen Defever reported that she has neither received nor spent any money this year.

Incumbent Councilmember Jack Ryan filed a statement Sept. 16 saying he expects to receive and spend less than $2,000 this year.

In a Sept. 22 text message, Ryan said he was accepting zero dollars in donations and “spending as close to that as possible” for his campaign.

The town posted Jafar’s disclosure on its election webpage Sept. 28. Jafar told The Ark in a Sept. 25 phone interview that he had submitted it Sept. 23 to Assistant Town Manager and Town Clerk Lea Dilena, who was out of the office, and that he had been unable to reach her since.

The disclosure reports $1,523.44 of his own money and a $2,000 contribution from the owners of downtown Tiburon restaurant Sam’s Anchor Cafe, listed as Sam’s Main St. It also lists $500 from Arup Banerjee, CEO of artificial-intelligence company Windfall; $100 from Elaine Mak; and $75 in unitemized contributions of less than $100.

Jafar reported spending $1,523 on VistaPrint postcards and about $13 in unitemized payments of less than $100.

item.title: Belvedere bends its plaque policy for gazebo builder Larry Hadley
item.description: Belvedere’s parks committee voted Sept. 17 to bend its residency guideline and put up a plaque honoring Larry Hadley, whose company built the Community Park gazebo.
item.content:encoded:
Belvedere’s parks committee has agreed to bend the city’s residency guideline for plaques to honor Larry Hadley, the contractor whose company built the Community Park gazebo for free.

The city’s Parks, Open Spaces and Lanes Committee voted 4-0 Sept. 17, with committee member Marika Bergsund absent, to put a plaque honoring Hadley on or near the gazebo. Public Works Director Antony Boyd suggested that its exact location, design and wording be worked out with Chair Charlie Harrington rather than the full committee.

Because no new structure is being installed, the plaque needs only a design-review exemption from the city before it goes up, Boyd told The Ark.

Former Belvedere Mayor Sandy Donnell, who submitted the request on behalf of a group of residents, proposed wording along the lines of “In gratitude for Larry Hadley for his dedication to Belvedere.”

Hadley’s company built the gazebo and donated it to the city for Belvedere’s 1996 centennial. Hadley personally built the gazebo’s cupola, then transported it by trailer and maneuvered it into place with a crane.

item.title: Crib Notes: Tiburon waterfront estate on Old Landing Road hits market for $17.5 million
item.description: A single-story waterfront home at 36 Old Landing Road in Tiburon, steps from a private beach on the bay, is on the market for $17.5 million.
item.content:encoded:
An Old Landing Road home in Tiburon with direct access to the bay is on the market for $17.5 million.

The five-bedroom, 4½-bathroom house at 36 Old Landing Road is a single-story modern estate that offers privacy while sitting steps away from a private beach, says listing agent Stephanie Lamarre of Golden Gate Sotheby’s International Realty in Greenbrae.

“I’ve been in the industry for 18 years, and I’ve never seen anything like it — at any price,” Lamarre says of the home, which was listed Sept. 10.

The home — nicknamed “La Casa Dei Quattro Orizzonti,” Italian for “the house of four horizons” — sits on San Francisco Bay near Paradise Cay, looking toward the East Bay. Built in 2006, it has 6,721 square feet of living space on a 5.34-acre lot.

item.title: Election 2026: Measure P childcare tax would raise $12.5 million a year for Marin programs
item.description: Measure P, a 15-year countywide parcel tax on the Nov. 3 ballot, would subsidize childcare in Marin and raise pay for providers, about $100 a year for a 2,000-square-foot house.
item.content:encoded:
Owners of a 2,000-square-foot house would pay about $100 a year for 15 years to subsidize childcare in Marin and raise pay for the people who provide it if county voters approve Measure P on Nov. 3.

The tax is 5 cents per square foot of what the ordinance calls structural improvements, meaning building floor area, with no more than 100,000 square feet of any single parcel taxed. Land is not taxed, only what is built on it, and beginning in the tax’s second year supervisors may raise it each year by the Bay Area consumer price index. The county estimates it would raise about $12.5 million a year, and there are no exemptions for seniors or low-income owners.

The ordinance directs the money to three things — subsidizing care for what it calls low- and middle-income children and families, raising provider pay and building and expanding facilities as needed — and sets no required share for any of them.

Election 2026: Read complete coverage at thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Money would go into a special county fund, and the Marin County Children and Families Commission, the nine-member body supervisors appoint, would write a five-year program plan and budget and allocate the proceeds. Supervisors would still have to appropriate the money each year, and they may replace the commission with another agency. The measure creates an 11-member advisory council, also appointed by supervisors, to recommend the plan and review an annual independent audit, and it caps administration at 5% of what the tax brings in.

Because Measure P, the Marin County Child Care Initiative, began as a citizens’ petition rather than as a measure proposed by the Marin County Board of Supervisors, it passes on a simple majority instead of the two-thirds California ordinarily requires of a special tax.

item.title: Election 2026: Measure CC hospital tax would raise $12.4 million a year for MarinHealth ER, ICU
item.description: Measure CC, a 30-year parcel tax on the Nov. 3 ballot, would pay for a larger ER and expanded ICU at MarinHealth Medical Center, Marin’s only trauma center.
item.content:encoded:
Marin’s only trauma center would get money for a larger emergency room and expanded intensive care under Measure CC, a 30-year parcel tax on the Nov. 3 ballot that would cost the owner of a 2,000-square-foot house $280 a year.

The Marin Healthcare District, which owns MarinHealth Medical Center, estimates the tax — 14 cents per square foot of building — would raise about $12.4 million a year. By Ark calculation, the owner of that 2,000-square-foot house would pay $8,400 over the life of the tax. There are no exemptions for seniors or for low-income owners. The measure’s backers say state law bars healthcare districts from offering a senior exemption.

Measure P, a separate countywide parcel tax on the same ballot, would charge 5 cents a square foot for 15 years to subsidize childcare and raise pay for childcare workers. If both measures pass, a property owner in the healthcare district, which includes Tiburon, Belvedere and Strawberry, would pay 19 cents a square foot between them — or $380 a year on a 2,000-square-foot house in the first year. Measure P’s share could rise each year with inflation; Measure CC’s is fixed. The county and the healthcare district project the two would raise about $24.9 million a year combined.

Election 2026: Read complete coverage at thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Measures CC and P are both special taxes, and the CC ordinance carries a clause saying that if it and a conflicting measure both pass, only the one with more yes votes takes effect. County Counsel Brandon Halter said the county does not believe CC would knock out P because the same clause lets measures that can be harmonized both take effect, and the two “impose separate taxes for different purposes and do not appear to impose inconsistent requirements.” A court would decide the question if it were challenged, he said.

Measure O, a $115 million Reed Union School District bond on the same ballot, would add to what Tiburon and Belvedere owners pay if it passes. It is levied on assessed value rather than building size, at an estimated peak of $30 per $100,000, or $300 a year for each $1 million of assessed value. Strawberry is outside the Reed district.

Like Measure P, Measure CC qualified by petition, which means it passes on a simple majority rather than the two-thirds a district-sponsored special tax would need.

item.title: Picks of the Week: Sample vintages at Tiburon Wine Festival; Jazz piano trio at Old St. Hilary’s Landmark
item.description: The Tiburon Wine Festival runs 1-4 p.m. Oct. 3 at Point Tiburon Plaza, and the Ben Stolorow Trio plays 4 p.m. Oct. 4 at Old St. Hilary’s Landmark in Tiburon.
item.content:encoded:
Sample vintages at Tiburon Wine Festival: The 43rd annual Tiburon Wine Festival runs 1-4 p.m. Oct. 3 at Point Tiburon Plaza, hosted by the Tiburon Peninsula Chamber of Commerce. Sample vintages from 60 established and small-batch wineries from across the state, along with food from 10 local eateries and live music from Mercy & The Heartbeats. Attendees must be 21 or older and bring valid government-issued photo identification. No infants, strollers or animals are allowed on event grounds. The festival will proceed rain or shine with no refunds. Proceeds support free chamber events such as the Tiburon Holiday Festival and Friday Nights on Main. Tickets are $139.49 including fees. tiburonwinefestival.com.

Jazz piano trio at Old St. Hilary’s Landmark: The Ben Stolorow Trio will perform at 4 p.m. Oct. 4 at Old St. Hilary’s Landmark in Tiburon. Stolorow, a member of the faculty of The Jazzschool in Berkeley, is a pianist with many influences, from Bach to Thelonious Monk and McCoy Tyner of the John Coltrane Quartet. Tickets are $20-$25 in advance online or at the Landmarks office at The Boardwalk shopping center, $25-$30 at the door if not sold out. There is no parking at Old St. Hilary’s; free parking is available at The Boardwalk shopping center, with a shuttle leaving from in front of Rustic Bakery beginning 30 minutes before the show. 415-435-1853 or landmarkssociety.com.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Hessel

item.title: Marin County to test AlertMarin emergency alerts at 10 a.m. Sept. 26; fewer than half of Tiburon, Belvedere households signed up
item.description: Marin County will test AlertMarin, its emergency notification system, at 10 a.m. Sept. 26, sending a test alert to everyone registered for the service.
item.content:encoded:
Marin County will test AlertMarin, its emergency notification system, at 10 a.m. Sept. 26, sending a test alert to everyone registered for the service.

The test checks that AlertMarin can get critical information out in an emergency, according to the county Office of Emergency Management, part of the Marin County Fire Department. Belvedere, in a notice urging residents to sign up, also cited the approach of peak wildfire season and the El Niño forecast.

Subscribers will get the test by whatever contact methods they chose — text message, phone call or email — in English or Spanish, depending on their account settings. Anyone who doesn’t receive it should log in at alertmarin.org and check that their contact information and addresses are current, the county said.

Fewer than half of Tiburon and Belvedere households will get it. In Tiburon, 1,782 households, or 48%, have a subscription, and in Belvedere 456, or 45.5%, according to the office’s AlertMarin subscriber dashboard.

The rate falls by more than half in multiunit properties, where just 110 of Tiburon’s 588 housing units, or 18.7%, and 29 of Belvedere’s 136, or 21.3%, have at least one household subscriber. Tiburon has 2,716 individual subscribers in all and Belvedere 675.

AlertMarin sends real-time instructions during wildfires, floods, evacuations and other emergencies that call for immediate action. Anyone who lives or works in Marin can register at alertmarin.org, which the county says takes less than five minutes, and list up to five addresses — the county suggests home, work, a child’s school and a family member’s or friend’s house.

Subscribers can also opt into Notification Groups for information that falls short of an emergency alert: significant weather, coastal flooding and king tides, creek and river flooding, prescribed burns and significant traffic disruptions. The groups are not location-based, so a subscriber gets every notice on a topic, wherever in the county it applies.

The county also recommends saving AlertMarin’s number, 877-627-1411, as a phone contact, letting it bypass Do Not Disturb settings and adding a home landline as a second contact method.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Hessel

item.title: Belvedere approves Marin’s first commercial drone delivery rules
item.description: Belvedere City Council voted 3-2 Sept. 14 to advance Marin’s first commercial drone delivery ordinance, barring delivery hubs from homes and limiting where drones can land.
item.content:encoded:
The Belvedere City Council has advanced Marin County’s first ordinance written specifically for commercial drone deliveries, approving it 3-2 after adding protections for public property and privacy.

Councilmembers Jane Cooper and Pat Carapiet voted against the ordinance Sept. 14 after arguing that its proposed delivery hours — beginning at 7 a.m. and extending as late as 11 p.m. — could disturb residents. Mayor Sally Wilkinson, Vice Mayor Kevin Burke and Councilmember Peter Mark supported the measure.

The ordinance is expected to return for a second reading Oct. 12. If adopted, it would take effect 30 days later.

The measure would regulate ground-level activity associated with commercial deliveries, including where drones may land, take off and leave packages. It would not regulate drones while they are in flight because airspace, flight paths, aircraft equipment and pilot requirements fall under the Federal Aviation Administration’s authority.

item.title: Election 2026: Strawberry Rec draws rare race for four-year seats
item.description: Four candidates are running for three four-year seats on the Strawberry Recreation District board Nov. 3, a rare contested race for a district that has struggled to fill seats.
item.content:encoded:
Four candidates are running for three four-year seats on the Strawberry Recreation District board Nov. 3, a rare contested election in a district that has long struggled to find anyone willing to serve.

Chair Peter Teese, a board member since December 2010, is seeking a fifth term. Fellow incumbent Sohrab Saghezchi, a Mill Valley dentist appointed to the board in December 2022 is standing for election to the seat for the first time. The only challenger is David Morgenthaler, a Strawberry father who spent nearly five years in sales and business development at Salesforce.

The fourth candidate, incumbent Sarah Waterfield, declined to comment and did not sit for a portrait.

Election 2026: The Strawberry Recreation District four-year candidates at a glance

Election 2026: Read complete coverage at thearknewspaper.com/election2026

The board voted unanimously Aug. 18 to reject a Marin County civil grand jury recommendation capping special-district members at two consecutive four-year terms, with Teese arguing the district almost never has a contested election and that a limit could empty a seat with no one waiting to fill it. Both of its races are contested this year.

Two other candidates, incumbent Doug Twillman and newcomer Aliza Hawkins, are running for the board’s single two-year seat.

The independent special district serves the unincorporated Strawberry community of about 6,000 residents. Under the board and General Manager Nancy Shapiro, it runs year-round programs, classes, memberships and events and oversees parks, including the dock at Harbor Cove Park. According to the district, property taxes supply only a fraction of its funding from local property taxes — 3.5 cents per dollar of basic tax paid to Marin County, or roughly 15% of its annual revenue. The rest, about $3 million, comes mostly from fees for classes, facility rentals and memberships.

The district hired playground company GameTime in July under a $2.4 million contract to build a playground on grass between the tennis courts and baseball fields at Strawberry Park. A revised quote and a separate bid for a restroom pushed the total past $3 million on Sept. 8, and the board told the company to come back under its $2.5 million ceiling. The playground is expected to open in 2027.

item.title: Election 2026: The Strawberry Recreation District four-year candidates at a glance
item.description: The Strawberry Recreation District four-year candidates at a glance
item.content:encoded:
David Morgenthaler, challenger

Years as resident: 5.

Occupation: Sales and marketing professional, formerly with Salesforce.

Education: Bachelor’s degree in music-industry studies from the University of Southern California.

Civic background: Member of the Strawberry Neighborhood Association; local activist on Flock Safety automated license-plate readers.

Key issues: New district programs, including teen programs and music and foreign-language classes.

Quote: “I’m trying to think outside the box for how we can serve more of the community.”

Sohrab Saghezchi, incumbent

Years as resident: 10.

Occupation: Dentist and owner of Mill Valley Dental.

Education: Studied biology at the University of California at Davis and San Jose State University; doctor of dental surgery degree from the University of the Pacific’s Arthur A. Dugoni School of Dentistry in San Francisco.

Civic background: Appointed to the Strawberry Recreation District board in December 2022.

Key issues: Transparency, fiscal responsibility and the new playground project slated for 2027.

Quote: “I think just making sure that (the district) is connected with the community and making sure that we’re listening to the community and obviously with this big project with the playground, we want to make sure that it’s something everybody is going to be proud of.”

Peter Teese, incumbent

Years as resident: 24.

Occupation: Western sales director at U.S. News & World Report.

Education: Bachelor’s degree in advertising from the University of Colorado Boulder.

Civic background: Member of the Strawberry Recreation District board since December 2010; board chair.

Key issues: The new playground project slated for 2027 and the potential to build an amphitheater near the recreation center’s elevator.

Quote: “There should be more programs that are either low cost or no cost for kids. I think (the new playground) really answers that.”

Sarah Waterfield, incumbent

Years as resident: 7.

Occupation: Told The Ark in 2024 she was senior vice president of global brand strategy at Ultragenyx, a Novato pharmaceutical company.

Education: Bachelor’s degree in history and literature from Harvard University and attended Stanford University’s Graduate School of Business.
